metadata.title: CONCEPTUAL CONSTRUCTION OF GLOBAL COMPETENCE IN EDUCATION

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a critical literature review and discourse analysis rather than an empirical analysis of ILSA microdata. Therefore, there is no student-level sampling frame, no plausible values (PV) generation, and no complex survey design to weight. The authors discuss PISA 2018’s inclusion of global competence and cite reported national results (e.g., Spain’s basic-level attainment), but they do not analyze a dataset with sampling weights. For any future empirical study using PISA microdata, analysts should apply the official student/sampling weights provided in the international database (and replicate weights if available) when estimating population-representative relationships.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is not an empirical microdata study: it synthesizes conceptual definitions, theoretical backgrounds, and discourse patterns about global competence. Because there is no student-level dependent variable measured via PISA cognitive scales, plausible values (PV) are not generated or analyzed, and missing-data handling for PVs is not part of the study design. The paper’s limitations concern conceptual and measurement comparability across frameworks, not statistical missingness in an analyzed dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Critical literature review and discourse analysis. The authors conducted a search in SCOPUS, Web of Science, and Dialnet using the descriptor “global* competen*” (and Spanish equivalents), selecting documents published in English and Spanish from 2001–2020, followed by bibliography tracking for chronological analysis. No student-level ILSA sample is constructed.

data.outcome_summary: This paper is a critical review and discourse analysis of how “global competence” has been conceptualized, with special attention to intercultural education as an inclusion-oriented educational approach. It discusses the OECD/PISA 2018 definition of global competence and contrasts conceptual “background ideas” (often aligned with social efficiency/human capital) versus “foreground ideas” (often aligned with social reconstructionism). The review highlights that global competence and intercultural competence are frequently used interchangeably, while global competence is argued to be more comprehensive for addressing globalisation challenges. It also emphasizes conceptual and measurement challenges that limit international comparability, including critiques of PISA 2018’s framework and the difficulty of standardizing assessment of a construct that is not purely science-based. The study does not report ML model performance metrics because it does not conduct predictive modeling on ILSA microdata.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction contains no empirical ML components because the manuscript is explicitly a critical literature review and discourse analysis rather than an analysis of ILSA microdata. As a result, there is no analytic sample size, no country-level student counts, no PV handling, and no survey-weighting or missing-data strategy to document. The study’s “results” are conceptual findings about dominant approaches and measurement limitations, so the main_findings table for predictive outcomes is intentionally empty.
